title: Planning-horizon dependence of sample complexity
formal: Let \(N(S,A,H,\varepsilon)\) be the smallest worst-case number of complete episodes sufficient to learn an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal policy with probability at least \(2/3\) in the class of time-homogeneous finite Markov decision processes defined below. Does the following proposed lower bound hold: there are universal constants \(c>0\), \(0<\varepsilon_0<1/4\), and integers \(S_0,A_0\ge2\), \(H_0\ge1\) such that for every \(S\ge S_0\), \(A\ge A_0\), \(H\ge H_0\) and \(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0\), \[N(S,A,H,\varepsilon)\ge c\,SAH/\varepsilon^{2}?\] This is the concrete scaling conjecture stated in the 2018 source. The parameters vary independently; a condition forcing the state count to grow with the horizon is not part of the claim.
why: This question separated the statistical cost of planning far ahead from changes in reward scale, state-space size and the unit used to count observations. Its negative resolution shows that long episodes alone need not force polynomially more episodes in the normalized tabular model, clarifying the limits of that model as an explanation of long-horizon difficulty.
status_note: Resolved negatively. Checked on 2026-09-14: the 2022 COLT paper explicitly recalls the 2020 refutation and proves a stronger horizon-independent PAC episode bound in the same time-homogeneous, nonnegative unit-total-reward model. The theorem and model scopes were checked, not independently formalized.

progress.text: Jiang and Agarwal conjecture a sample lower bound proportional to the horizon under time-homogeneous dynamics and a unit bound on total episode reward.
Wang, Du, Yang and Kakade explicitly refute polynomial horizon dependence by obtaining only logarithmic dependence in sample complexity.

Zhang, Ji and Du prove a polynomial-time horizon-free result. Theorem 1 and its PAC consequence remove even logarithmic horizon dependence from the episode bound, at the cost of nonoptimal state and action factors.

sentences: The original conjecture asserted a linear planning-horizon factor in the number of episodes needed for tabular reinforcement learning.
The environment has time-homogeneous transitions and rewards, while an output policy may depend on the time step.
Rewards are nonnegative and their total in each episode is bounded by one.
Published results refute polynomial horizon dependence and subsequently remove horizon dependence from the episode bound entirely.
The historical question is resolved, while optimal dependence on other parameters is a separate target.

definitions:
For positive integers \(S,A,H\), states are \([S]=\{1,\ldots,S\}\), actions are \([A]\), and every episode has exactly \(H\) steps. An unknown model consists of an initial distribution \(\mu\) on \([S]\), a transition distribution \(P(\cdot\mid s,a)\) on \([S]\), and a reward distribution \(R(\cdot\mid s,a)\) on \([0,1]\). These three objects do not depend on the time step or episode. Each episode starts afresh from \(\mu\); at each step, conditional on the current state and chosen action, the observed reward and next state are independent draws from their respective kernels, with fresh randomness across steps and episodes. At the last step only the reward is needed. Impose the additional promise that the sum of rewards in every episode is at most one almost surely under every policy. This permits individual rewards larger than \(1/H\).

The learner knows \(S,A,H,\varepsilon\), observes states and rewards, and may choose actions using all previous observations and its independent randomness. Its only access to the model is through complete episodes; there are no queries at chosen state–action pairs or resets inside an episode. A policy to be returned is a deterministic table \(\pi:[S]\times[H]\to[A]\), so it can vary with the time step although the environment is time-homogeneous. Write \(V_M(\pi)=\mathbb E_M[\sum_{t=1}^{H}r_t]\) and \(V_M^*=\max_{\pi}V_M(\pi)\). Success means \(V_M(\hat\pi)\ge V_M^*-\varepsilon\). For a fixed parameter tuple, \(N\) is the least integer \(n\ge0\) for which one learning rule uses at most \(n\) episodes on every observation history and succeeds on every promised model; set it to \(+\infty\) if none exists. Probability includes the environment and learner randomness. The target is statistical sample complexity, with no computational-time bound. Count episodes, each containing \(H\) interactions, rather than individual transitions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universally quantified lower bound. A refutation must prove that every proposed set of constants fails for some admissible parameter tuple. In particular, a proved sample-complexity upper bound independent of \(H\), with the other parameters fixed, refutes it. The published negative resolution is recorded below; this archival status does not assert that a Lean formalization has already been supplied.

context_blocks.text: A long episode supplies more observations as well as more decisions. Counting individual transitions would automatically introduce a factor equal to the horizon. The source instead counts full episodes and bounds the entire episode reward by one, so its proposed lower bound concerns an additional statistical difficulty.

Time-homogeneous dynamics allow information about a state and action to be reused at different times. Allowing separate transition laws at each time would introduce additional unknown parameters and would change the question. Optimal policies can nevertheless be nonstationary because the remaining number of steps matters.

The 2022 theorem gives a regret bound with polynomial state and action dependence and no horizon dependence. Its stated PAC consequence uses at most a polynomial in the state count, action count and inverse accuracy, again independent of the horizon. Holding those parameters fixed contradicts the proposed linear horizon lower bound.

This conclusion does not identify the optimal dependence on all the remaining parameters. It also does not imply that executing or storing a long policy takes constant time: the episode count and computational work are different resources.
